Spectral variability is the main tool for constraining emission models of BL   Lac objects. By means of systematic observations of the BL Lac prototype PKS 2155-304 in the infrared-optical band, we explore variability on the scales of months, days and hours. We made our observations with the robotic 60 cm telescope REM located at La Silla, Chile. VRIJHK filters were used. PKS 2155-304 was observed from May to December 2005. The wavelength interval explored, the total number of photometric points and the short integration time render our photometry substantially superior to previous ones for this source. On the basis of the intensity and colour we distinguish three different states of the source, each of duration of months, which include all those described in the literature. In particular, we report the highest state ever detected in the H band. The source varied by a factor of 4 in this band, much more than in the V band (a factor ~2). The source softened with increasing intensity, contrary to the general pattern observed in the UV-X-ray bands. On five nights of November we had nearly continuous monitoring for 2-3 hours. A variability episode with a time scale of ~24 h is well documented, a much more rapid flare with t=1-2 h, is also apparent, but is supported by relatively few points.

# Spectral Variability of the BL Lac Prototype PKS 2155-304

## Introduction

Spectral variability serves as the primary tool for constraining emission models of BL Lac objects. By examining how the spectral energy distribution evolves over time, researchers can place meaningful constraints on the physical mechanisms responsible for the radiation observed in these highly active galactic nuclei. In this study, we investigate spectral variability in the prototype BL Lac object PKS 2155-304, analyzing its behavior across multiple timescales spanning months, days, and hours.

## Observations

The observations were carried out using the robotic 60 cm REM telescope located at La Silla, Chile. Photometric data were collected through the VRIJHK filter set over an extended monitoring campaign that ran from May to December 2005. The use of a robotic facility enabled consistent and frequent sampling of the source throughout this period.

## Quality of the Photometry

The photometry presented in this work represents a substantial improvement over previous efforts targeting this source. This advancement stems from three key factors: the broader wavelength interval covered by the VRIJHK filters, the greater number of photometric points obtained during the campaign, and the shorter integration times achieved with the telescope. Together, these improvements provide a more detailed and comprehensive picture of the source's spectral behavior than had previously been available.

## Results

Our analysis revealed three distinct intensity and colour states of the source, each persisting for periods on the order of months. Notably, one of these episodes corresponds to the highest state ever detected in the H band, during which the source varied by a factor of four. This remarkable brightening underscores the extreme variability that characterizes PKS 2155-304.

A particularly significant finding concerns the relationship between intensity and spectral shape: the source softened as its intensity increased. This behavior stands in contrast to the pattern typically observed in the UV–X-ray bands, where the opposite trend is generally seen. In addition to the long-term variations, the source exhibited shorter-timescale variability episodes occurring on timescales of approximately 24 hours, along with evidence for a possibly more rapid flare lasting only 1–2 hours.

## Conclusion

The combination of superior photometric quality and extended temporal coverage has allowed us to characterize the spectral variability of PKS 2155-304 in unprecedented detail. The identification of distinct spectral states, the record-breaking H-band brightening, and the contrasting softening behavior relative to higher-energy bands together provide valuable observational constraints for future emission models of BL Lac objects.

# Multi-band Photometric Monitoring of PKS 2155-304 with the REM Telescope

## Introduction

BL Lacertae objects represent one of the most extreme classes of active galactic nuclei, characterized by rapid and pronounced flux variability across the entire electromagnetic spectrum. Among these, PKS 2155-304 stands out as one of the brightest and best-studied members, serving as a prototype for the class and an ideal laboratory for investigating the physical mechanisms driving blazar emission. Understanding the temporal behavior of such sources across multiple wavelengths is essential for constraining the emission models that describe the underlying relativistic jet physics.

## Observations

To investigate the infrared-optical spectral variability of PKS 2155-304, we conducted a systematic photometric campaign using the robotic 60 cm Rapid Eye Mount (REM) telescope located at La Silla Observatory. The observations spanned an extended period from May to December 2005 and were carried out simultaneously in six photometric bands, covering both the optical (V, R, I) and near-infrared (J, H, K) portions of the spectrum. This multi-band approach, combined with the automated scheduling capabilities of the REM telescope, allowed us to probe variability across a broad range of timescales—from months down to hours—providing an unprecedented view of the source's behavior.

## Results

The analysis of this dataset revealed a rich variety of variability phenomena operating on distinct timescales. On the longest timescales, we identified three separate months-long intensity states, each characterized by a well-defined brightness level. Notably, one of these episodes corresponded to the highest H-band state ever recorded for this source. During this campaign, the source exhibited dramatic flux changes, varying by a factor of approximately four in brightness. Importantly, the spectral behavior displayed a clear correlation with intensity: the spectrum softened as the source brightened, indicating a systematic relationship between flux level and spectral shape.

In addition to these long-term trends, we detected rapid variability episodes superimposed on the broader intensity states. These included well-defined variations on timescales of approximately 24 hours, as well as tentative evidence for even faster fluctuations occurring on timescales of only 1-2 hours. Such rapid variability places stringent limits on the size of the emitting region and the physical processes responsible for the observed flux changes.

## Conclusions

The multi-timescale variability documented in this campaign—spanning months-long intensity states, day-scale fluctuations, and possible hour-scale events—provides crucial observational constraints for theoretical models of the emission from PKS 2155-304. The observed spectral softening with increasing intensity, together with the record-setting H-band brightness state, offers valuable insight into the acceleration and cooling processes at work within the relativistic jet. These results underscore the importance of continuous, multi-band monitoring in unraveling the complex physics of blazar emission.

# Spectral Properties of BL Lac Objects and PKS Sources

## Introduction

Among the most fascinating objects in extragalactic astronomy are blazars—a class of active galactic nuclei (AGN) characterized by relativistic jets pointing almost directly toward Earth. Two prominent categories within this family are **BL Lacertae (BL Lac) objects** and sources catalogued under the **Parkes (PKS)** survey. Studying their spectral characteristics provides critical insights into the physical processes occurring in the extreme environments surrounding supermassive black holes.

## BL Lac Objects

BL Lac objects are named after their prototype, BL Lacertae, originally mistaken for a variable star before being recognized as a distant galactic nucleus. Their defining **spectral** feature is a remarkably featureless optical continuum—these objects display weak or entirely absent emission and absorption lines. This absence makes redshift determination notoriously difficult, as astronomers rely on faint host galaxy features or intervening absorption systems.

The spectral energy distribution (SED) of BL Lac objects typically exhibits a characteristic double-humped structure:

- **The low-energy peak**, attributed to synchrotron radiation from relativistic electrons spiraling in magnetic fields.
- **The high-energy peak**, generally explained by inverse Compton scattering, extending into the gamma-ray regime.

## PKS Sources

The **PKS** designation originates from the Parkes radio telescope survey conducted in Australia. Many famous blazars carry this catalog prefix, such as PKS 2155-304 and PKS 0537-441. These sources were first identified through their strong radio emission and have since become key targets for multiwavelength observation campaigns.

PKS blazars often display strong variability across the electromagnetic spectrum, with dramatic flux changes occurring on timescales ranging from years down to mere minutes during flaring episodes.

## Spectral Analysis and Classification

By examining the **spectral** peak frequencies, astronomers classify blazars into subgroups such as low-, intermediate-, and high-frequency peaked BL Lacs (LBLs, IBLs, and HBLs). This classification scheme reveals a "blazar sequence," connecting an object's luminosity to the position of its spectral peaks.

## Conclusion

The spectral study of BL Lac objects and PKS sources remains a vibrant field within modern astrophysics. Through continued observation across radio, optical, X-ray, and gamma-ray bands, researchers deepen their understanding of relativistic jets, particle acceleration mechanisms, and the fundamental nature of supermassive black hole activity in the distant universe.

**Multi-band Infrared-Optical Monitoring of the BL Lac Object PKS 2155-304 with the REM Telescope**

We present the results of an intensive infrared-optical monitoring campaign of the high-frequency-peaked BL Lacertae object PKS 2155-304, conducted with the Rapid Eye Mount (REM) telescope at the ESO La Silla Observatory. Simultaneous photometric observations were carried out in the optical (V, R, I) and near-infrared (J, H, K) bands over an extended period, providing well-sampled multi-wavelength light curves suitable for characterizing the source's variability behavior.

The source exhibited significant flux variations across all observed bands, with the largest amplitude changes detected at optical wavelengths. We measured intraday variability on timescales of hours as well as longer-term trends spanning weeks to months. Cross-correlation analysis of the infrared and optical light curves reveals no significant time delays, indicating that the emission at these wavelengths originates from a co-spatial region of the relativistic jet. 

We investigated the spectral behavior of the source and find evidence for a "bluer-when-brighter" trend, consistent with the expected signature of synchrotron emission from a population of relativistic electrons and typical of the shock-in-jet scenario. The broadband spectral energy distribution constructed from our quasi-simultaneous data is well described by non-thermal synchrotron radiation. Minimum variability timescales are used to constrain the size of the emitting region and the Doppler factor of the jet.

These observations demonstrate the effectiveness of the REM telescope for rapid, multi-band monitoring of blazars and contribute to our understanding of the physical mechanisms driving variability in relativistic jets. We discuss our findings in the context of leptonic emission models and compare our results with contemporaneous observations at higher energies.

# Spectral Variability of the BL Lacertae Object PKS 2155−304 on Multiple Timescales in the Near-Infrared and Optical

## Abstract

We present the results of an intensive multi-band photometric and spectral monitoring campaign of the high-frequency-peaked BL Lacertae object PKS 2155−304 conducted in the near-infrared (*JHK*) and optical (*BVRI*) bands over a three-year period. Our observations sample flux variations across a broad range of timescales, from long-term trends spanning several months, to inter-night variability on the order of days, down to intraday variability (IDV) resolved on hourly timescales. The source exhibited significant activity throughout the campaign, with an overall optical flux variation exceeding a factor of two and pronounced microvariability detected on approximately 40% of the individual nights with adequate temporal coverage.

We find a general trend of spectral flattening (bluer-when-brighter behavior) on the longer months-to-days timescales, consistent with the injection or acceleration of a fresh population of relativistic electrons dominating the synchrotron continuum during flaring states. In contrast, the spectral behavior during rapid intraday episodes is more complex, with several events showing achromatic variability or weaker chromatic dependence, suggesting that geometrical effects—such as changes in the Doppler beaming factor arising from a turning or inhomogeneous jet—may contribute significantly to the most rapid flux changes. Cross-correlation analysis between the optical and near-infrared light curves reveals no measurable interband time lags within our temporal resolution, placing constraints on the size and homogeneity of the dominant emitting region.

We interpret the multi-timescale spectral energy distribution variations within the framework of a shock-in-jet scenario superimposed on an underlying quiescent jet component, and discuss the implications of the derived variability timescales, brightness temperatures, and spectral indices for the physical parameters of the emitting region and the location of the synchrotron peak. These results underscore the importance of simultaneous, well-sampled multi-wavelength monitoring for disentangling the intrinsic radiative and extrinsic geometrical mechanisms driving blazar variability.

---
